doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: What jazz means to him: musical conversation on the bandstand
summary: Davern laments the decline of instrumental music and describes the joy of musical conversation.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah, they do abound. But I mean there’s so much that you could talk about, only thing is it’s such a drag because nobody really — maybe they’ll care about it in a hundred years or whatever, these things.

Maybe. If anybody really cares to listen to it. But it’s just so sad to see the whole thing ending. Instrumental music as we know it. Just stay home and practice your instrument and go, try to get a beautiful sound and articulation and play music that you can experience with other guys on the bandstand, which I don’t find happening anymore either, you know. To find a trade off of ideas and just like conversational — it’s so rare. To have fun and to make musical conversation. But there’s no feeling like it when it’s happening. None like it. I mean when you’re dancing it doesn’t matter what the chords are, nothing matters, it’s just that you are dancing and you can do no wrong, and every interval has — it’s a very rare thing but once it’s happening to you you’re hooked. And that’s what jazz music means to me.
The music swells up behind us. Nice statement. Just to wrap up here.
